Female Genital Mutilation (Arabic: ختان المرأة) is the practice of cutting away and altering the external female genitalia for ritual or religious purposes. It can involve both or either Clitoridectomy and Excision. Clitoridectomy is the amputation of part or all of the clitoris or the removal of the clitoral prepuce. Excision is the cutting away of either or both the inner and outer labia. A third practice, Infibulation (or Pharaonic circumcision), is the paring back of the outer labia, whose cut edges are then stitched together to form, once healed, a seal that covers both the openings of the vagina and the urethra. Infibulation usually also includes clitoridectomy.

FGM predates Islam. The Banu Quraysh, Muhammad's native tribe, appear to have engaged in the practice. Muhammad maintained the practice after migrating to Medina and is recorded as approving of the practice in four hadith. Two hadith record the sahabah (Companions of Mohammed) engaging in the practice (see FGM in the Hadith).

The FGM hadith give very few clues as to the nature of the practice they approve. Hence the nature, incidence and distribution of FGM varies between countries and communities. The most significant determining factor appears to be the presiding school of Islam (fiqh). Other factors include the culture's level of anxiety around female sexuality, its proximity to Islamic slave-trade routes (Infibulation is associated with the transportation of slaves), and the nature and degree of Christian influence.

Whilst the Qur'an contains no explicit mention of FGM, verse 30:30, by exhorting Muslims to 'adhere to the fitrah' indirectly, but ineluctably, exhorts Muslims to engage in FGM (see FGM in the Qur'an).

Islamic law also implicitly favors FGM by creating social conditions that 1/ make the practice useful or necessary, and 2/ normalise it. Polygyny (which Islam encourages) creates sexually violent societies which put girls and women at a heightened risk of rape or abduction. In response to this the community develops practices which safeguard the 'purity', chastity and reputation of its girls and women. FGM is such a practice - as are child marriage, gender segregation and purdah, arranged marriages, chaperoning, veiling, 'honour' culture, bride-price (mahr) and footbinding. Islam's legitimisation of slavery, especially sex slavery, also has a significant role in the nature, incidence and distribution of FGM.

Traditional scholars all allow, recommend or mandate FGM (see FGM and the Schools of Islamic Law). Whilst most modern fatwas favour FGM, there has been, over the past half century, a growing unease in the Islamic world concerning the practice (due to a growing concern on the part of organisations such as the UN and UNICEF). This has resulted in some fatwas critical of FGM. It appears that the earliest fatwa clearly critical of FGM was issued in 1984. (see Modern Fatwas)

It should be noted that those who practice FGM refer to it as Female Circumcision rather than Female Genital Mutilation. The Hadith and most of the fatwas reproduced on this page are translations. Where this is the case it is likely that the term used is the translator's choice, not the hadith or fatwa's originator.

FGM is mentioned in (at least) seven Hadith. Four report Muhammad approving of FGM and two report Sahabah (Muhammad's companions) participating in FGM. The remaining hadith has little import doctrinally, but is of linguistic, historical and sociological interest.

Abu Hurayrah said: I heard the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allaah be upon him) say: “The fitrah is five things – or five things are part of the fitrah – circumcision [الْخِتَانُ - khitan], shaving the pubes, trimming the moustache, cutting the nails and plucking the armpit hairs.”

Sahih Bukhari 7:72:777; See also Sahih Muslim 2:495


Hadith methodology dictates that if it is not mentioned specifically or if the pronouns do not point to a certain gender, then the hadith is valid for both sexes (either directly or by analogy, or qiyas, in the case of women). Hence, this hadith is applicable for both men and women.

A Preservation of Honor for Women

Abu al- Malih ibn `Usama's father relates that the Prophet said: "Circumcision [الْخِتَانُ - khitan] is a law for men and a preservation of honour for women'."

Ahmad Ibn Hanbal 20:719; Al-Baihaqqy 8:324

Do Not Cut Severely

Narrated Umm Atiyyah al-Ansariyyah: A woman used to perform circumcision [الْخِتَانُ - khitan] in Medina. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said to her: "Do not cut severely as that is better for a woman and more desirable for a husband".

comment_text:
Debate Analysis

TL-DR: Charlie focuses on marriage and children from a spiritual lens while Tilly focuses on improving societal expectations and supports from a social lens. Since they spoke from different lenses, they weren't able to properly address each-other's questions. My comment summarises Charlie and Tilly's positions, provides quotes and timestamps, compares the positions, shows observations of the debate going wrong, and closes with a statement.

What should the role for women in public and private life look like? What are the material benefits of that?

Charlie posits that women's role be wife and mother; that women have an inherent desire to get married and have children which is necessary in positively affecting well-being among them (3:25). He claims that in Western countries, women who are married and having children are happier than their counterparts (4:51), and that women's suicide rates are higher while marriage rates are lower compared to that of Sub-Saharan African countries which observes the opposite (5:49). He says that deviating from this inherent desire is what is negatively affecting well-being. Being a wife and mother in society can be supported by observations of higher happiness, life meaning, and life satisfaction.

Tilly posits that society ought to be made more fair and supportive of women to improve their social experience. She claims that women's stress and dissatisfaction comes from the dual pressures of outdated expectations in society [excelling in both career and domestic labor] (1:50). She attributes women's dissatisfaction to certain economic policies, income inequalities, lack of social cohesion, and social health (3:40). She focuses on maximizing agency within a fair system with helpful, economical, morally good parameters (5:11). She also says that society can structurally support women through policies (e.g universal childcare and shared legally reinforce-able parental leave) (8:20). 

Charlie --> Marriage, Children, Faith in the Divine
Tilly --> Remove unfair social pressures, provide structural social supports to women, explore other moral scales for women

While marriage, children and worship is a specific goal, the improvement of social experiences among women is a broad one.

While Charlie places an emphasis on getting married, having children and having faith in the divine, Tilly places an emphasis on removing harmful social pressures and adding social supports. While Charlie focuses on this inherent drive to take on a particular role (wife and mother), Tilly focuses on optimizing the social experience of women through more socioeconomic ways. While Charlie attributes women's dissatisfaction to deviating from marriage and children, Tilly attributes it to unfairness in policy and lack of social health. While Charlie focuses on the psychological and spiritual implications of marriage and children, Tilly focuses on the socioeconomic factors to make women's experiences more fair, supported and do-able.

Once, Tilly displayed distrust in happiness surveys (5:22), and then displayed trust in happiness surveys advocating for structural supports (8:24).

Once, Charlie asked Tilly if married mothers in the West were happier, to which she said "I would have to look into it" (4:18). As they speak on, Tilly then focuses on agency, fairness and reasonable parameters. Later on, Tilly displays distrust in African women suffering gender mutilation checking "happy" on a survey (6:30). Because of that, they couldn't properly talk about marriage and children. Tilly mostly talked about socioeconomic factors and structural supports, which Charlie wasn't prepared for either. Because of that, Charlie and Tilly spoke from different realms and struggled to get onto the same page.

As the debate was closing, Tilly said that Charlie's moral scale of value is biological (e.g birth rate), and that her own moral scale of value is social; being a mother is biological while being a good nurturer is social. She then asks why Charlie's moral scale would be top priority, to which Charlie focuses on happiness, life meaning and life satisfaction (9:28).

Neither of them "won" or "lost". They both had very different perspectives. They both had excellent insights which people can learn from. Psychologically and spiritually, women's role in public-private life could be to live with purpose, perhaps in marriage, children and in worshipping the divine. Socioeconomically, women's role in public-private life can be improved by removing barriers and providing supports.

comment_text:
@birdwaveracing9 

If “answering at a higher standard” means redefining what counts as an answer whenever the original question becomes inconvenient, then the standard isn’t higher it’s undefined. For example “Answering at a higher standard” would mean committing to whether surveys are valid or not. She didn’t do that. She treated them as unreliable when they showed decline, but still leaned on the same type of subjective self report studies when it helped her case. That isn’t depth. What that is is refusing to freeze the metric. You can call that good delivery, but it isn’t a better answer. And to try and make it seem like she did that on purpose because she’s like “playing 4d chess and using Charlie’s own tactics against” him is corny and silly. 

Every serious debater prepares questions, anticipates evasions, and uses constrained framing to force commitments. that’s not unique to Charlie, it’s the craft. Binary questions aren’t bad-faith by default; they only become bad-faith if clarification is disallowed afterward. What you’re calling “bad-faith” here is really just pressure you don’t like applied asymmetrically. For example they condemn Charlie for framing questions to expose weaknesses while praising her for framing answers to avoid exposure. That’s not a principled objection to bad faith. If “being prepared” were inherently illegitimate, it would disqualify most top debaters across law, academia, and public debate. It doesn’t. What’s being objected to here isn’t the method, but who is using it.

When people say “intellectuals” in this way, they usually mean a narrow social class, not a methodological one. People who share the same priors. People who already accept certain frameworks as settled. People for whom signaling alignment matters as much as, and often more than, argument quality. The reaction to her Valium comment makes it clear that it was echo-chamber reinforcement intoxicated on no substance sound bites.

Saying academics would be “somewhat unimpressed” by her is doing an extraordinary amount of work. Somewhat is far too generous. From a genuinely academic lens, her performance had three fatal problems:
	•	No frozen metrics
	•	No falsifiability
	•	No causal commitments

That doesn’t make her evil or stupid. It makes the argument methodologically weak.
Academia does not reward:
•	Narrative substitution for evidence
Example
“So I would argue that what you’re calling unhappiness is actually visibility, because now we hear women expressing dissatisfaction, whereas in the 50s, we prescribed them valium and we lobotomized.”
Why this qualifies
	Charlie asked a trend question (are women happier now vs 40 years ago). Instead of addressing the empirical comparison, she substitutes: a historical narrative,
•	Treating disagreement as pathology
Example 
“I don’t think happiness is a very good metric, and neither do you, because you think gay people shouldn’t just pursue happiness by being gay. They have other moralistic considerations to be making.”
Why this qualifies
The disagreement over metrics is reframed as a revelation about Charlie’s moral psychology.
His empirical question becomes evidence of:
•	moral inconsistency,
•	ideological motivation,
•	or bias.
•	The metric itself still isn’t resolved.
This is psychologizing the opponent instead of answering the claim.
•	Answering empirical questions with moral posture
Quote
“I don’t think smiles per capita is a particularly convincing way to measure whether or not we should encourage women to be autonomous. I think we should maximize agency within a fair system… because it’s the moral thing.”
Why this qualifies
•	The empirical question is: Do certain life choices correlate with higher happiness?
•	Her response:
•	dismisses the metric,
•	pivots to moral justification (“we should maximize agency”),
•	and reframes the debate as what we ought to value.
•	Whether the correlation exists is never answered.
That’s moral posture substituting for causal analysis.

Charlie, for all his flaws, honestly started in good faith. She didn’t. Her first move was to treat the sex–gender separation framework as settled, without acknowledging its empirical failures or ethical costs, while framing dissent as unserious.

The John Money framework is not neutral: It is historically contested, It has documented victims, Its core claims were never empirically validated in the way she treats them as “obvious.” Presenting that framework as axiomatic isn’t intellectual rigor. Once you do that, every subsequent exchange is skewed because challenges become moral failings, evidence becomes irrelevant, and evasion is recast as sophistication.

She didn’t “dissect” him. she evaded his questions. Dissection requires engaging the claim under a fixed metric. What she did instead was substitute narrative, moral framing, or meta-commentary whenever the question became constraining. I wouldn’t call her a debater I would call her a rhetorical Houdinist.

The Valium comment is a good example, and yes, he let it slip by. That was an execution failure on his part. But that doesn’t make the move incisive. The comment replaced an empirical question about trends in reported happiness with historical imagery and moral shock. It should have been frozen immediately and forced back to the metric. It wasn’t, and she benefited from that lapse.

Importantly, a missed enforcement doesn’t retroactively turn evasion into argument. She didn’t win that exchange by offering clarity; she won it because the substitution went unchallenged. That’s not really the surgical dissection you’re describing it’s more like exploiting a dropped guard.

The pause later in the debate was entirely justified. She had just spent several minutes explaining why self reported happiness surveys are deeply flawed, then immediately cited those same surveys when they supported her claim. Stopping the exchange there wasn’t rudeness or incompetence; it was an attempt to restore consistency that should have happened earlier.

What’s being praised here isn’t intellectual rigor, but the ability to change standards mid stream without being forced to commit. You can argue that works for internet audiences. You can’t argue that it constitutes dissection. Dissection answers questions. Evasion avoids them
